15-076.r: Cruise missiles → jet-propelled throughout flight (subsonic, supersonic or hypersonic); ballistic missiles → rocket-powered only in boost phase. BrahMos = supersonic cruise missile; Agni-V = solid-fuelled intercontinental ballistic missile.
15-076.t: The question swaps both pairs: don't call Agni-V a cruise missile or BrahMos a ballistic missile.

15-077.r: BrahMos → supersonic cruise missile, joint venture of India (DRDO) and Russia (NPO Mashinostroyenia); speed 2.8–3.0 Mach; original range 290 km.
15-077.h: BrahMos = Brahma(putra) of India + Mos(kva) of Russia.

15-081.r: 18 October 2020 → Naval version of BrahMos supersonic cruise missile test-fired from stealth destroyer INS Chennai, hitting a target in the Arabian Sea.

15-082.r: BrahMos: supersonic cruise missile built with Russia; test-fired 21 March 2010 from INS Ranvir off Odisha; range 290 km (450/500 km after 2019). So 22 March, 400 km are wrong.

15-083.r: BrahMos (290 km) first tested January 2009 at Pokhran, Rajasthan; land-attack Block-II tested 29 March 2009 from a Mobile Autonomous Launcher at Pokhran.

15-084.r: April 2024 → India delivered first batch of BrahMos to the Philippines, its first export customer ($375-million deal, January 2022). Reason (490 km range) is false.

15-085.r: Lakshya → India's first unmanned aircraft, developed by the Aeronautical Development Establishment (ADE) of DRDO.
15-085.t: Don't pick INS Virat (aircraft carrier) or Sukhoi (fighter); only Lakshya is unmanned.

15-086.r: Netra → 1.5 kg unmanned aerial vehicle by DRDO's Pune labs and Idea Forge, for anti-terror and counter-insurgency work; flies up to 200–300 metres.

15-087.r: UAV types: multi-rotor, fixed-wing, single-rotor, fixed-wing hybrid VTOL. Only multi-rotor and VTOL/hybrid land vertically, so no 'all UAVs' statement (vertical landing, hovering, battery-only) is correct.

15-088.r: Avani Chaturvedi → first Indian woman IAF pilot to fly MiG-21 Bison solo, 20 February 2018.

15-089.r: F-18 Super Hornet → American fighter built by Boeing, flies day and night; used by US Navy, Royal Australian Air Force, Kuwait Air Force, not 'eight countries'.

15-090.r: AESA radar → multimode, solid-state active phased array fire-control radar with wide band RF front end, fits various fighter aircraft; it can track multiple targets.

15-091.r: THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) → American anti-ballistic missile system; destroys short, medium and intermediate-range missiles in terminal phase by hit-to-kill (no warhead).

15-092.r: Iron Dome → Israel's mobile all-weather air defence (lower layer); made by Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries; intercepts short-range rockets and artillery shells.
15-092.t: Not USA or France: THAAD is the American system, Iron Dome is Israeli.

15-093.r: Fractional Orbital Bombardment System → missile placed in stable low-Earth orbit, then deorbits (retrograde burn) over a target on Earth.

15-094.r: START-I and START-II → Strategic Arms Reduction Treaties between USA and USSR.

15-095.r: New START → bilateral strategic nuclear arms reduction treaty, USA–Russia; signed 8 April 2010 in Prague by Medvedev and Obama.

15-096.r: India supports FMCT negotiations in the CD ('does not support' is wrong); India is party to CWC and all five CCW protocols (signed 1981, ratified 1984); not a CTBT signatory.

15-097.r: 1 June 2016 → India joined the Hague Code of Conduct (HCoC) against ballistic missile proliferation; members now 145.

15-098.r: Australia Group (1985) → informal group to curb exports aiding chemical/biological weapons; 43 members incl. all 27 EU states, USA, Canada. Both statements wrong.

15-099.r: NATO → 32 members (30 European, 2 North American), HQ Brussels; North Atlantic Treaty signed in Washington, 4 April 1949. '42 members' is wrong.

15-100.r: Sweden → 32nd NATO member on 7 March 2024 after about 200 years of neutrality (since Napoleonic Wars); joined Partnership for Peace in 1994.
15-100.t: Finland joined NATO earlier; the 'about 200 years of neutrality' clue points to Sweden.

15-101.r: Operation Pawan (late 1987) → IPKF operation to take Jaffna (Sri Lanka) from the LTTE under the Indo-Sri Lanka accord.

15-102.r: DefExpo-2022 (12th edition, Gandhinagar, Gujarat, 18–22 October 2022) → theme 'Path to Pride'. DefExpo is biennial; first held 1999.

15-103.r: IONS (Indian Ocean Naval Symposium) → launched by Indian Navy in February 2008; voluntary forum for maritime cooperation among Indian Ocean littoral navies. Not 2015.

15-104.r: Friendship (Druzhba)-2016 → Russia–Pakistan joint military exercise, 24 September–10 October 2016, at Cherat, Pakistan.

15-105.r: Malabar 2017 (21st edition, 10–17 July, near Chennai) → navies of India, USA and Japan; Australia joined in 2020, making it quadrilateral.

15-106.r: Maitree → India–Thailand joint military exercise (2016 edition at Krabi, Thailand, 15–29 July).

15-107.r: Milan → Indian Navy's premier multilateral exercise; Maldives refused India's invitation to Milan-2018 (10th edition, Andaman Sea).

15-108.r: SLINEX → Sri Lanka–India Naval Exercise; SLINEX-II held at Trincomalee, September 2011.

15-109.r: Harimau Shakti → India–Malaysia joint military exercise (2018 edition at Hulu Langat, Malaysia).

15-110.r: AFINDEX-2023 (2nd Africa-India Field Training Exercise) → Aundh, Pune, 16–29 March 2023; 25 African nations took part.

15-111.r: Mitra Shakti → India–Sri Lanka (not Bangladesh) army exercise; 2023 edition at Aundh, Pune, 16–29 November, with IAF personnel; aim: joint counter-terrorism response.

15-112.r: JIMEX-24 (eighth Japan-India Maritime Exercise) → Yokosuka, Japan, June 2024; India sent stealth frigate INS Shivalik.

15-113.r: CINBAX (India–Cambodia joint table-top exercise), 1st edition → Foreign Training Node, Pune, 1–8 December 2024; counter-terrorism under UN Charter Chapter VII.

15-114.r: Khanjar → India–Kyrgyzstan special forces exercise; Khanjar-XII held in Kyrgyzstan, 10–23 March 2025.

15-115.r: Wrong pair: Thailand – Yudh Abhyas; Yudh Abhyas is India–USA. Correct: Indra–Russia, Khanjar–Kyrgyzstan, Lamitiye–Seychelles, Maitree–Thailand.
15-115.c: The book's explanation ends 'pair of option (c) is incorrect', but its own table shows (d) Thailand – Yudh Abhyas is the wrong pair; answer (d) is right.

16-001.r: Machine gun → James Puckle, an English London solicitor, patented his 'Defence Gun' in 1718, a key step towards mechanical machine guns.

16-003.h: Galileo, 1609: thermoscope and telescope, same man, same year.

16-004.r: Microscope → used to see micro (very small) and nearby objects that the naked eye cannot see.

16-005.r: Typewriter → Sholes (1867); X-ray → Wilhelm Roentgen (1895); Radio → Marconi (1901); Safety lamp → Humphry Davy (1815).

16-007.r: William Henry Bragg shared the 1915 Physics Nobel with his son William Lawrence Bragg; together they built the X-ray spectrometer for crystal structure.

16-008.r: Gutenberg → printing press; W.C. Roentgen → X-ray; Michael Faraday → dynamo; Alexander Graham Bell → telephone.

16-009.r: Steam engine → James Watt (major improvements); earlier Thomas Savery patented a steam pump for mines (1698), improved by Thomas Newcomen (1712).

16-011.r: Electric bulb → Thomas Alva Edison, American scientist.

16-012.r: Gas engine → Gottlieb Daimler (1885); diesel engine → Rudolph Diesel (1895).
16-012.t: Don't pick Diesel for the gas engine; Diesel made the diesel engine ten years later.

16-013.r: Fountain pen → Lewis Edson Waterman, New York, 1883; patented first practical fountain pen in 1884.
16-013.t: Parker, Sheaffer and Chelpark are pen brand names; the inventor is Waterman.

16-014.r: Radar (Radio Detection and Ranging) → Scottish physicist Robert Alexander Watson; first radar system 1935, used by Britain's Royal Air Force in World War II.

16-015.r: Dynamite → Alfred Nobel, Swedish scientist; Nobel Foundation set up from his will in 1900.

16-016.t: Galileo → telescope, not television; Edison → electric bulb.

16-018.r: Laser → Theodore Maiman; first shown working on 16 May 1960 with a ruby crystal at Hughes lab, Malibu.

16-019.r: Penicillin → Alexander Fleming (Scottish), not J. Perkins. Correct pairs: James Watt – steam engine; A.G. Bell – telephone; J.L. Baird – television.

16-024.r: Radium → Pierre and Madam Curie (1898); Penicillin → Alexander Fleming (1928); X-ray → W.C. Roentgen (1895); Edward Jenner → vaccine (1796).
16-024.c: The book pairs Edward Jenner with measles; Jenner's 1796 vaccine was for smallpox, not measles. Code (a) is still the only one that fits.

16-026.r: Order of invention: Diode (J.A. Fleming, 1904) → Transistor (1947, Bardeen, Brattain, Shockley, Bell Labs) → Integrated Circuit (Kilby, Noyce) → SMD (IBM, 1960s).

16-027.r: Alfred Nobel → dynamite; Alexander Fleming → penicillin (1928, from fungus Penicillium notatum); Charles Darwin → theory of evolution; Madam Curie → isolation of radium.

16-028.r: Black hole principle / Chandrasekhar Limit → S. Chandrasekhar: a white dwarf cannot be stable above 1.44 times the Sun's mass. His Nobel field: astrophysics.

16-030.r: Stars below 1.44 times the Sun's mass end as white dwarfs; white dwarf mass cannot exceed 1.44 solar masses → S. Chandrasekhar (Chandrasekhar Limit).

16-031.r: Photoelectric effect (electrons emitted from metal when light falls on it) → discovered 1887 by German physicist Heinrich Rudolf Hertz; also called Hertz effect.
16-031.t: Hertz discovered it; Einstein later explained it and won the Nobel for it.

16-032.r: Einstein → Nobel Prize in Physics 1921 for the law of the photoelectric effect, explained using Planck's quantum theory.
16-032.t: Einstein's Nobel was not for relativity.

16-037.r: Theory of relativity → Albert Einstein: special relativity 1905, general relativity 1915.

16-038.r: E = mc² → E = energy, m = mass, c = speed of light; mass and energy are equivalent.

16-039.r: Albert Einstein played the violin (and piano).

16-040.r: Time as the fourth dimension (with length, width, depth) → Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity, 1905.

16-041.r: C.V. Raman → Physics Nobel 1930 (first Asian) for scattering of light, Raman Effect. National Science Day, 28 February, marks the Raman Effect discovery (1928).

16-046.r: National Science Day (28 February) marks C.V. Raman's discovery of the Raman Effect, not any scientist's birthday; Raman was born 7 November 1888.
16-046.c: The book gives no single answer (*): the question is wrong, as no option's birthday is National Science Day.

16-047.r: C.V. Raman (born 7 November 1888, died 21 November 1970) → birth centenary celebrated in 1988.
16-047.t: Ramanujan was born 1887 and Darwin 1809, so 1988 fits only Raman.

16-048.r: 'The Man Who Knew Infinity' (2015 British film, from Robert Kanigel's 1991 book) → life of mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan, played by Dev Patel.

16-049.r: New Theory of Relativity → J.V. Narlikar, with Fred Hoyle, by amending Einstein's Theory of Relativity.

16-050.r: Astrophysicist Jayant Vishnu Narlikar → astrology is not a science.

16-051.r: Father of India's nuclear (atomic energy) programme → Homi Jehangir Bhabha.

16-052.r: Homi Bhabha Award → for special contribution to nuclear energy, in memory of Bhabha, father of India's nuclear energy programme.

16-053.r: Stephen Hawking (8 January 1942 – 14 March 2018) → British theoretical physicist and cosmologist, known for black hole work; suffered from ALS.

16-054.r: Jagdish Chandra Bose → research in both biology and physics (radio and microwave signals); invented the Crescograph to measure plant growth.

16-055.r: Raja Ramanna → nuclear physics; M.S. Swaminathan → agricultural science (Father of Green Revolution); U.R. Rao → space research (ex-ISRO chief); Meghnad Saha → thermodynamics and astrophysics.

16-056.r: Thermal ionization of gases → Meghnad Saha (papers of 1920–1921); explains the Sun's spectrum and stellar spectra.

16-057.r: India's atomic bomb → Dr. Raja Ramanna; supervised first nuclear test 'Smiling Buddha' (1974); later DRDO Director General.
16-057.t: Bhabha founded the nuclear programme; the 1974 bomb test is linked with Ramanna.

16-058.r: Jagdish Chandra Bose never won a Nobel. Winners: Har Gobind Khorana (Medicine 1968), C.V. Raman (Physics 1930), S. Chandrasekhar (Physics 1983).

16-059.r: 2023 Physics Nobel → Pierre Agostini, Ferenc Krausz, Anne L'Huillier for attosecond light pulses to study electron dynamics. 2024 → Hopfield and Hinton (machine learning).

16-060.r: 2023 International Prize in Statistics ('Nobel of statistics') → C.R. Rao (Calyampudi Radhakrishna Rao), Indian-American statistician; prize given every two years.

17-001.r: Quantum Mechanics → branch of physics dealing with the motion of very small particles.

17-002.r: Geodesy → science of measuring Earth's geometric shape, orientation in space and gravity field, and their changes with time; book's answer is (e) None/More than one.

17-003.r: Cybernetics → study of control and communication in animal and machine (defined by Norbert Wiener, 1948).

17-004.r: Horology → art or science of measuring time.

17-005.r: Tribology → study of friction and lubrication; a branch of mechanical engineering and material science.

17-006.r: Plasma (fourth state of matter) → charged particles (ions, electrons) formed when gas is heated very strongly; abundant in stars like the Sun. LED light is not plasma.

17-007.r: White Dwarf (Degenerate Dwarf) → a topic of astronomy.

17-008.r: Wrong statement: blue scatters more than violet. Violet scatters more; sky looks blue from strong scattering of violet, indigo, blue. Conducting aircraft tyres, earthing ropes on fuel trucks are correct.

17-010.r: National Chemical Laboratory (CSIR-NCL) → Pune; set up 1950; a CSIR laboratory.
17-010.t: NPL is in New Delhi; NCL is in Pune.

17-011.r: Tata Institute of Fundamental Research → Mumbai; founded by Homi Bhabha on 1 June 1945 with support from Sir Dorabji Tata.

17-012.r: LASER → Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation; a device producing stimulated radiation by optical amplification.
17-012.c: The book's note says Russians N.S. Basov and A.M. Prokhorov built the first laser in 1960; the first working laser (ruby) was built by Theodore Maiman in 1960.

17-014.r: First laser → ruby laser by Theodore H. Maiman, Hughes Research Laboratories, 1960; gives pulses of deep red light (694.3 nm), not blue.

17-016.r: Revolver → Samuel Colt; Dynamite → Alfred Nobel; Law of Cooling → Newton; Law of Pressure → Pascal.

17-017.r: Torch dry cell → zinc anode and carbon cathode.

17-018.r: ATM → Automated Teller Machine; used for bank transactions like cash withdrawal and statements.

17-019.r: All ATMs in India are linked by the National Financial Switch (NFS), run by NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India); NFS was built by IDRBT in 2004.

17-020.r: Nanotechnology → science and technology at nanoscale, about 1–100 nanometres (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m); can work wonders in device miniaturisation.

17-021.r: Nanoparticle → at least one dimension below 10⁻⁷ m; size range 1–100 nm (10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁷ m).
17-021.h: Nano = 10⁻⁹; a nanoparticle is 1 to 100 of those.

17-023.r: Nanoparticles also occur naturally (geological, biological processes, interplanetary dust); metal-oxide nanoparticles are used in some cosmetics; some reaching the environment are unsafe for humans.

17-024.r: Nano plug → a tiny, almost undetectable hearing aid with micro components and a nano-battery, programmed through computer software.

17-025.r: Nanoear (2012, Munich University, Germany) → an optically trapped gold nanoparticle; detects sound as low as –60 dB.
17-025.t: Gold nanoparticle, not silica or silver; –60 dB, not –120 dB.

17-026.r: Term 'Nanotechnology' → Norio Taniguchi, professor at Tokyo University, first used it in a 1974 research paper.

17-027.r: Carbon nanotubes (cylindrical carbon allotropes) → carry drugs and antigens in the body, used in biochemical sensors, biodegradable; making artificial blood capillaries is not correct.

17-028.r: Nanotechnology in health → makes targeted drug delivery possible and contributes largely to gene therapy (both true).

17-029.r: India's first nano-cellulose plant (ICAR-CIRCOT, Mumbai) → cotton; uses cotton linters and cotton waste as raw material.

17-030.r: IIT Roorkee's nano-fabrication facility (Uttarakhand's first) → supports Semiconductor, Nano and Quantum Missions; it is not linked to Samudrayaan.

17-031.r: Most important property of nanomaterials (as per the book) → friction.

17-032.r: One dimension in nano range → quantum well; two dimensions → quantum wire; all three dimensions → quantum dot.
17-032.h: Well, wire, dot: shrink one, two, then all three dimensions.

17-033.r: Quantum dot → semiconductor nanostructure, about 1.5–10.0 nm, with size-dependent optical and electronic properties.

17-034.r: Nanotechnology generations: I aerosols, colloids → II targeted drugs, 3-D transistors → III robotics, 3-D networking → IV molecular manufacturing. Order A, D, B, C.

17-035.r: Nano Hummingbird (Nano Air Vehicle) → tiny remote-controlled spy aircraft that looks and flies like a hummingbird; made by AeroVironment Inc., USA.

17-036.r: First successful tapping of underground heat → Boise, Idaho, USA (1890), using a hot-water pipe network to heat buildings.

17-037.r: Enron Power Project → Dabhol, Ratnagiri district, Maharashtra; built by Enron, GE and Bechtel; now owned by Ratnagiri Gas and Power, an NTPC subsidiary.

17-038.r: Amarkantak thermal power station → Chachai, Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh; coal-fired, run by MPPGCL.

17-039.r: 88th Indian Science Congress (New Delhi, 3–7 January 2001) → theme 'Food, Nutrition and Environmental Security'.

17-040.r: Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2020 → proposed 'One Nation, One Subscription' and RIEF; Atal Innovation Mission is not its outcome (launched 2016).

17-041.r: CSIR Award for S&T Innovations for Rural Development 2006 → Central Leather Research Institute (CLRI), Chennai.

17-042.r: Padma Vibhushan 2023 (Science and Engineering) → S.R. Srinivasa Varadhan, Indian-American mathematician (probability, large deviations); first Asian Abel Prize winner, 2007.

17-043.r: Vinod Dham → 'Father of the Pentium Chip' (led Intel's Pentium microprocessor); Padma Bhushan 2025 for Science and Engineering.

17-044.r: ICSSR (Indian Council of Social Science Research) → not a science and technology body. DST, CSIR, DAE are S&T bodies.

17-045.r: National Innovation Foundation–India → autonomous body of the Department of Science and Technology (since March 2000), backing grassroots innovation and traditional knowledge, not elite foreign-linked research.

17-046.r: Chevron → oil; AT&T → telephone, internet; AMD → microprocessor; Enercon GmbH → wind energy.

17-047.r: Dakshin Gangotri (1984) → India's first permanent Antarctic research station; Maitri (1989) second; Bharati third and newest (Larsemann Hills, Prydz Bay).
17-047.h: D-M-B: Dakshin Gangotri, Maitri, Bharati in time order.

17-051.r: IndARC → India's first multi-sensor underwater moored observatory, in Kongsfjorden, Arctic (between North Pole and Norway); deployed 23 July 2014.
17-051.t: IndARC is in the Arctic; Antarctic stations are Dakshin Gangotri, Maitri, Bharati.

17-052.r: Samudrayaan → India's first manned deep ocean mission (under Deep Ocean Mission); 6,000 m depth in manned submersible MATSYA 6000.

17-053.r: CANI (Chennai–Andaman & Nicobar) submarine optical fibre cable → dedicated to the nation by PM Modi on 10 August 2020; foundation stone 30 December 2018, Port Blair.

17-054.r: Titan → submersible of American firm Ocean Gate that imploded on 18 June 2023 during a dive to the Titanic wreck, North Atlantic, off Newfoundland, Canada.

17-055.r: Polar Code → IMO's mandatory international code of safety for ships operating in polar waters, under SOLAS and MARPOL.

17-056.r: Uttarakhand's first Doppler Weather Radar → Mukteshwar, Nainital district (January 2021), under the Integrated Himalayan Meteorological Project of the Ministry of Earth Sciences.

17-057.r: Isohaline → line of equal salinity in the ocean, not snowfall. Isobar → equal pressure; isoheight → equal height; isobath → equal underwater depth.

17-058.r: Pycnocline → sea water density (correct pair). Thermocline → rapid temperature change with depth in ocean (not air); Halocline → salinity; Ecocline → gradual change between ecosystems.

17-059.r: Density gradient in water → Pycnocline. Halocline → salinity gradient; Thermocline → temperature transition layer between surface and deep water.
17-059.h: Pycno = dense, Halo = salt, Thermo = heat.

17-060.r: 'I am a citizen of the Milky Way' → Kalpana Chawla, astronaut on STS-107 (Columbia), killed when it broke up on re-entry.

17-061.r: India's first heavy water plant → Nangal, Punjab (1962), in National Fertilisers Limited premises, set up by the Department of Atomic Energy.

17-062.r: Oxygen → paramagnetic (weakly attracted by a magnetic field). Other paramagnetic ones: platinum, sodium, aluminium, manganese, potassium, chromium.
17-062.t: Iron is ferromagnetic (strongly attracted), not merely paramagnetic.

17-063.r: Aluminium → paramagnetic, barely attracted by a magnet. Iron, nickel and cobalt → ferromagnetic, strongly attracted.
17-063.h: Ferromagnetic trio: Iron, Nickel, Cobalt (Fe, Ni, Co).

17-064.r: Copper → non-magnetic (non-electromagnetic) element; nickel, cobalt, chromium are not.

17-065.r: Magnetic (compass) needle → points north; its north end lines up with Earth's magnetic field.

17-066.r: Tape recorder tape → plastic coated with ferromagnetic powder (tiny iron particles) that gets magnetised during recording.

17-067.r: Most accurate atomic clock (loses one second in 300 million years) → strontium atoms; made at JILA (NIST and University of Colorado), USA.

17-068.r: Automatic wrist watch → powered by movements of the wearer's hand, no battery; stops if not worn for 2–3 days.

17-069.r: Electronic watch → crystal oscillator plays the pendulum's role (timekeeping); vibrates at natural frequency under alternating voltage (inverse piezoelectric effect).

17-070.r: Quartz crystal in watches → piezoelectric effect: certain materials produce electric charge under mechanical stress.

17-071.r: MOEMS → Micro-Opto-Electro-Mechanical Systems (optical MEMS); e.g. optical switches, microbolometers.

17-072.r: PUMA (robotics) → Programmable Universal Machine for Assembly; industrial robot arm by Victor Scheinman at Unimation, first made for General Motors.

17-073.r: Radar (radio detection and ranging) → used for monitoring precipitation (weather radar) and tracking animal migration (birds, insects); not for spotting narcotics on passengers. So only two.

17-074.r: Drones can spray pesticides on crops, inspect active volcano craters and collect breath samples from spouting whales for DNA analysis → all three.
